transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-12-15 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Drew Chen (Redwood SE), Luis Moreno (CTO - Pegasus), Aisha Khan (ML Lead), Tom Bishop (Platform Eng)
---
Summary: quick intro, qualification, technical constraints, model + context discussions, tooling questions, security/compliance, recap + next steps.

[00:00] Samira: hey everyone, thanks for joining. i'm samira, i'm the account exec and i'll drive the high level stuff today. with me is drew chen, our systems SE. how are you all?
[00:05] Luis: good, thanks. we've got about an hour. trying to figure out if redwood hosted or a dedicate, or private deploy makes sense for us. big drivers are context length, multilingual, and tool-calling.
[00:18] Aisha: yes also latency for interactive product and cost targets, we do around 1.2M inference tokens per day in peak.
[00:26] Drew: thanks, that helps. quick clarifying q — are your prompts mostly single turn or long multi-turn threads with state?
[00:32] Aisha: long threads, we need history + large doc retrieval — some interactions need 40k to 60k of context, like multi-doc extraction and chain-of-thought.
[00:41] Tom: plus we must keep certain logs on prem, for compliance reasons, and any PII must not leave our region for EU customers.
[00:50] Samira: ok good, that's the three big constraints. i'll run through options fast: hosted API for fast time-to-value, dedicated for predictable throughput and isolation, and private for VPC or on-prem where you need full control.
[01:03] Luis: queue — can hosted do 64k?
[01:06] Drew: hosted can run large-context models — depends on model variant. we have variants we've verified at 32k and 64k contexts for several open models, but for production we usually recommend dedicated or private if you need sustained high-concurrency at 64k because of GPU memory pressure and cost predictability.
[01:18] Aisha: what's the difference in cost if we keep everything hosted vs move to dedicated? ballpark.
[01:22] Samira: rough rule — hosted is usage-based, you pay per-token and it's simpler. dedicated is table-stakes for throughput: monthly reserved capacity, lower per-token cost at scale, but commit. we'll send a rough estimate. drew will include the batch sizes/kv cache settings.
[01:33] Drew: to add, we use KV cache and prefix caching to reduce repeated token compute. that matters with long context retrieval patterns. note some transcription systems call it kv cash sometimes — sorry that's, that was me —
[01:45] Luis: (laughing) kv cash, noted.
[01:48] Aisha: model wise we were evaluating LLaMA derivatives, pg-13 evals... sorry, i mean, llama 2 variants, mosaicml, and a couple of LLMs from Cohere. we also looked at Anthropic's longer context models. any recommended open models for 64k plus tool-calling?
[02:03] Drew: for open models at very long context, we've had good results with trimmed/finetuned variants of Llama2-Chat-32k and some newer 64k checkpoints (community builds). there's also some Eleuther family builds but quantization quality can vary. important tradeoff: larger context + quantization can produce hallucinations if model isn't adapted. for tool-calling, model must support structured output reliably — we validate tool schemas in evals.
[02:42] Aisha: do you support progressive windowing? like operate on 8k windows and stitch? because some of our retrieval pipelines already chunk texts to 8k.
[02:49] Drew: yes, you can do sliding window strategies or KV cache where we keep long-term KV and feed incremental tokens. our runtime supports continuous batching and smart KV eviction policies. for best latency, dedicated pools often give more predictable latency and better KV cache effectiveness.
[03:08] Tom: about tool-calling — we have webhooks that trigger internal services and a runbook workflow. latency constraint is 400ms p50 for front-end interactive features. can redwood guarantee that with dedicated?
[03:21] Samira: we publish SLO ranges — dedicated SLA has tighter latency predictability. 400ms p50 is aggressive if you include network hops + tool-calls; often you see token generation p50 under 200ms for shorter context models on dedicated pools, but with long context generation times increase. we can architect a hybrid flow: short prompt for routing + async job to enrich — depends on UX.
[03:46] Luis: we want synchronous UX for some features though — so it's a tradeoff.
[03:51] Drew: one approach — use a smaller low-latency policy model to generate the immediate UI response while raising a background call with the large-context model to produce the deep answer; then update UI when ready. Redwood supports multi-model routing and fallback.
[04:08] Aisha: multilingual — we need Spanish, German, FR, Japanese and occasional Arabic. tokenization and vocab coverage are important — should we pick a single multilingual model or language-specific families?
[04:20] Drew: single multilingual models simplify ops; but per-language quality often better with region-specific models. for scale though, a high-quality multilingual 32k or 64k variant is a good starting point. we'll provide language-specific evals. also watch out for tokenization drift — some community multilingual finetunes drop tokens in rare scripts.
[04:43] Luis: security — we need SOC2, ISO27001, SSO/SAML, RBAC, KMS integration for encryption at rest, and audit logs. also want to avoid customer PII leaving our VPC for EU customers.
[04:57] Samira: we can provide SOC2 report and ISO summary. for EU data residency we have private deployment options: either VPC private control plane or on-prem package. KMS/HSM integration is supported on private deployments. we'll send docs.
[05:14] Tom: can you operate a private control plane that still allows your managed runtime to schedule inference, or does private mean fully self-managed?
[05:22] Drew: private has two flavors: VPC private control plane (Redwood control plane runs in a customer VPC with peered access) and fully on-prem where you run the orchestration stack. the VPC private gives us ability to push updates while keeping data within your network perimeter. on-prem is air-gapped variant but then ops responsibilities shift to you.
[05:42] Aisha: for benchmarks — what do you need from us?
[05:45] Drew: sample prompt sets, sample docs, concurrency profile, and languages. we'll run a matrix: 8k vs 32k vs 64k with typical batch sizes, quantization levels (fp16, q4, q5), and measure latency, p50/p95, tokens/sec, memory use, and quality metrics on your test prompts.
[06:06] Luis: how does quantization affect hallucinations? we've seen q4 result in odd tokenization artifacts on legal text.
[06:12] Drew: quantization trades off fidelity; some models are more robust. we recommend doing model-specific evals — sometimes q5 or mixed precision for large context yields better stability. Redwood Optimize can recommend quant profiles per workload.
[06:29] Tom: any third-party infra required? like do we need to provision GPUs in our cloud?
[06:34] Samira: if you pick hosted, no. for dedicated you'll procure reserved capacity through Redwood (we map to GPU pools on our infra). for private on-prem, yes you'll run on your infra. for VPC private we can broker cloud region capacity with our partners.
[06:51] Aisha: data retention — can we keep transcripts for 30 days? audit logs longer?
[06:55] Drew: yes retention is configurable per account; for private deployments retention stays in your control. hosted has standard retention but enterprise packs let you extend.
[07:05] Luis: who else at redwood will we work with on the pilot?
[07:08] Samira: you'll have a small REDWOOD success lead and the SE (drew) will run the benchmarks; our research team helps with evals.
[07:16] Aisha: about model updates — if we pin a version for rollout, can we do canary and A/B?
[07:20] Drew: yes, rollouts are first-class; canary deploys, A/B rollouts, automatic fallback policies are supported. you can pin model versions per route.
[07:29] Tom: what about tool-calling security — preventing an LLM from calling arbitrary endpoints?
[07:34] Drew: we enforce allow-lists, signed webhook tokens, and schema validation. calls go through Redwood routing and can be audited. we also support sandboxing for unknown tools.
[07:45] Luis: competitor concerns — we've been talking to anthroptic and open-ai as well. any differentiator?
[07:50] Samira: ours is production-first inference focus — unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private, transparent perf profiles, and tooling for cost/perf tradeoffs. Plus our optimize recommendations are workload-driven.
[07:59] Aisha: ok if we summarize next steps — we'll share sample prompts and docs, we want a benchmark for 64k context and a cost compare, and redwood to send security pack.
[08:10] Samira: exactly. drew you'll own the benchmark plan?
[08:13] Drew: yes i'll propose a matrix by next thursday.
[08:17] Tom: schedule the private deployment deep dive for Jan 6? works for us.
[08:21] Samira: i'll calendar that and include our infra eng.
[08:24] Luis: any blockers on our side? i don't think so.
[08:27] Aisha: nothing immediate — will gather examples.
[08:30] Samira: perfect. thanks everyone. we'll follow up with notes and the docs.
[08:36] (end, informal chatter on logistics)
